runs.text: - Revenue grew, but its mix shifted toward Retail: nine-month sales rose 4.3%, with Retail up 21.9% and Banking down 1.9% on the earnings-release presentation. Retail’s lower reported gross margin means growth can add scale while diluting margin if the gap persists. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7, 16; EX99.1_2026-09-30_dbd_ex-991q32026erlive-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9, 13; calculation C01; calculation C08

- Cash conversion weakened sharply: nine-month operating cash flow and free cash flow were negative USD 29.3 million and USD 68.5 million, respectively, after positive USD 83.2 million and USD 43.3 million in the prior-year period. Even excluding discrete taxes, the issuer’s free-cash-flow measure remained negative at USD 36.2 million. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 9–13; EX99.1_2026-09-30_dbd_ex-991q32026erlive-htm.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation C03

- Leverage increased mainly because cash fell, not because reported carrying debt surged: carrying-value net debt rose by USD 213.2 million from year-end 2025 to USD 764.4 million, and net leverage reached 2.33x. The company’s own USD 791.5 million net-debt figure uses gross debt before financing fees; the carrying-value measure is used here for leverage. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 54, 78; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C02

- Adjusted EBITDA is materially above reported EBITDA: the nine-month gap was USD 127.5 million, or 57.95% of reported EBITDA. Restructuring charges, the Turkey operation and an investment impairment account for major adjustments, so reported EBITDA is the more conservative base for leverage and cash-conversion analysis. Basis: EX99.1_2026-09-30_dbd_ex-991q32026erlive-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 14–16; calculation C04

- The USD 454.8 million unrestricted cash and net committed availability buffer, alongside known revolver and note maturities in 2029 and 2030, reduces immediate refinancing pressure. It does not establish covenant headroom or the maturity of USD 26.4 million of unidentified other long-term debt. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18, 23; 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 78–80; calculation C05

cells.text: Nine-month revenue was USD 2,816.8 million, up 4.3%; Banking USD 1,960.6 million (69.6% of revenue), down 1.9%; Retail USD 856.2 million (30.4%), up 21.9%
Retail growth offsets weaker Banking demand but moves mix toward the lower-margin segment
Nine months 2026: services USD 1,654.2 million (58.7%); products USD 1,162.6 million (41.3%)
The service stream supports installed-base work; hardware and project delivery remain sensitive to customer spending cycles
Nine months 2026 gross margin: Banking 26.4%; Retail 21.3%
A larger Retail mix can dilute gross margin if the differential persists
FY2025: EMEA USD 2,051.5 million (53.9%), Americas USD 1,460.6 million (38.4%), APAC USD 293.6 million (7.7%); no customer exceeded 10% of FY2025 sales
Geographic breadth limits reliance on one region, while EMEA concentration exposes results to regional demand, currency and regulation

Management reported orders for 500-plus cash recyclers, a 360-recycler Latin American branch win, 1,450 ATMs, about 1,200 POS lanes across 200 stores, 6,000 self-checkout units and a service agreement above USD 25 million
Supports sales activity and market access; delivery timing and earnings contribution are not quantified
Nine months 2026 free-cash-flow use USD 68.5 million; nine months 2025 free cash flow USD 43.3 million
Weaker cash generation makes working-capital recovery and discretionary spending more important to liquidity

Management lowered adjusted EBITDA guidance from USD 510–535 million to USD 490–510 million and free cash flow from USD 255–270 million to USD 190–210 million; revenue guidance is USD 3.86–3.90 billion versus USD 3.86–3.94 billion previously
Lower expected earnings and cash flow reduce the internally funded cushion for investment and debt service
The company expects to complete the Turkey wind-down by year-end 2026 and is exploring an exit from an unconsolidated Chinese investment
Exit costs, timing and proceeds are not fully quantified; execution and impairment risk remain

runs.text: Strength 1: Services were 58.7% of nine-month sales; maintenance and integration activity supports the installed base, which can sustain revenue and cash receipts across equipment cycles, although contract duration and renewal rates are not supplied. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation C07

Strength 2: No customer exceeded 10% of FY2025 sales and revenue spans Banking and Retail; this reduces single-customer dependence, though EMEA remains the majority region and segment demand is not equally profitable. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 5–10, 99

Strength 3: The completed refinancing established senior secured notes due in 2030 and an undrawn revolver due in 2029; the maturity profile provides time to recover cash generation, but market access and covenants remain untested. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 78–80; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18

Weakness 1: Nine-month FCF was negative USD 68.5 million and the cash-flow statement showed USD 174.6 million of use from listed asset-and-liability changes; collections, inventory turns and tax timing therefore drive near-term debt-service liquidity. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 9–13; calculation C03; calculation C06

Weakness 2: Retail growth is occurring at a lower gross margin than Banking, while reported product margins are under memory-cost and mix pressure; continuing this mix shift can lower earnings before fixed costs and cash interest. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, page 4; EX99.1_2026-09-30_dbd_ex-991q32026erlive-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 8–9; calculation C09

Weakness 3: Share repurchases of USD 148.6 million in nine months and an additional USD 19.3 million after quarter-end were made alongside negative free cash flow; further execution would reduce the cash retained for operations and deleveraging. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 19, 25; EX99.1_2026-09-30_dbd_ex-991q32026erlive-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C03

The evidence does not establish an owner-driven strategy or covenant breach; the weaknesses describe issuer-level financial policy and operating cash flow only. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 5–10, 79–80, 99; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 9–13, 17–19, 25; EX99.1_2026-09-30_dbd_ex-991q32026erlive-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2, 7–9; calculation C03; calculation C05; calculation C07

runs.text: The company and certain U.S. and Canadian subsidiaries filed prepackaged Chapter 11 cases on June 1, 2023; a Dutch scheme proceeded alongside them. The U.S. court confirmed the plan on July 13, the Dutch court sanctioned its plan on August 2, and both plans became effective on August 11, 2023. The company emerged using fresh-start accounting; the former common shareholders received less than half of the successor’s new common shares. This reset separated the predecessor and successor financial reporting, but the filing does not provide current beneficial-holder percentages. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 64–66

On December 18, 2024, Diebold Nixdorf issued USD 950 million of 7.75% senior secured notes due March 2030 and entered a USD 310 million revolving facility due December 18, 2029. The company used the note proceeds, a USD 70 million revolver borrowing and cash on hand to repurchase the emergence term loans, repay the prior revolver and pay related fees and premiums. The new notes and revolver share first-priority collateral; specified subsidiaries guarantee both facilities. The Q3 2026 filing reports that USD 37 million was drawn and repaid on the revolver during the first nine months of 2026, with no revolver balance at quarter-end. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 79–80; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dbd.htm.jsonl, pages 17–18

fields.value: Revenue reached USD 2,816.8 million in 9M 2026, up 4.3% year over year, but growth was concentrated in Retail: 9M Banking revenue declined 1.9% while Retail rose 21.9%. This exposes the credit story to product mix: Retail growth supports scale, while lower Banking product volumes and Q3 product-margin pressure can offset higher product volumes and pricing. Services gross margin benefited from VAT credits and execution, but those credits are not a repeatable substitute for durable product economics.

fields.value: Reported EBITDA was USD 220.0 million for 9M 2026, while adjusted EBITDA was USD 347.5 million. The USD 127.5 million gap comprises USD 78.2 million of restructuring and savings expenses, USD 16.9 million of investment impairment, USD 10.8 million for the non-core Turkey operation and other issuer-listed items. These adjustments raise the headline measure by 58% versus reported EBITDA; their scale makes sustainable cash earnings less certain, especially because the non-core Turkey adjustment removes a loss and restructuring savings are not yet fully realized.

fields.value: The cash conversion break is clearer than the adjusted EBITDA trend: 9M 2026 operating cash flow was negative USD 29.3 million and FCF was negative USD 68.5 million, compared with positive USD 83.2 million and USD 43.3 million, respectively, in 9M 2025. Inventory, deferred revenue, tax and payroll movements drove a net USD 174.6 million cash use in the listed asset and liability changes; cash flow before those movements was USD 145.3 million. Debt service capacity therefore depends on collections, inventory turns and timing of tax payments, not adjusted EBITDA alone.

LTM cash-interest cover was 4.27x, below FY2025’s 5.51x but above FY2024’s 2.18x; lower annual cash interest after the December 2024 refinancing improved cover, while the Q3 2026 cash decline weakened net leverage.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Diebold Nixdorf’s public operating model combines an installed service base with cyclical banking and retail hardware; for creditors, that mix diversifies revenue but leaves cash generation exposed to project timing and discretionary capital returns. Nine-month 2026 revenue grew 4.3%, led by Retail growth as Banking declined, while the company reduced its full-year earnings and free-cash-flow outlook. Services remained the larger revenue stream, but reported cash conversion was weak and share repurchases continued. The filings identify no current controlling shareholder in this evidence set, so sponsor alignment and shareholder control cannot be assessed from issuer identity or historic restructuring alone.

fields.value: Retail growth shifted the revenue mix toward a lower-margin segment: Retail contributed 30.4% of nine-month 2026 sales and grew 21.9% year over year, while Banking contributed 69.6% and declined 1.9%. The mix supports growth but can pressure consolidated gross margin if lower Retail margins persist.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The company’s disclosed nine-month 2026 free-cash-flow use was USD 68.5 million, and it repurchased USD 148.6 million of shares during the period, followed by USD 19.3 million of additional purchases through October 23. Those cash uses reduce the liquidity retained for working capital and investment while management has lowered its full-year free-cash-flow outlook.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The 2023 restructuring changed the equity base and accounting perimeter: the former shareholders received less than half of the successor’s new common shares, and fresh-start accounting made the reorganized company a new reporting entity. Current beneficial holders, their percentages and any sponsor rights are not identified in the supplied filings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Q3 customer wins across Banking and Retail support a constructive demand case, including orders for cash recyclers, ATMs, point-of-sale lanes and self-checkout refreshes. The release gives units and some contract values but not a complete delivery schedule, contribution margin or conversion into cash; these wins therefore support activity rather than a quantified near-term earnings bridge.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The company has a global installed base, no customer above 10% of annual sales in FY2025, a majority of revenue from services, and Q3-reported customer wins in both segments. This moderates single-customer and hardware-only concentration concerns. The outlook reduction, negative nine-month cash generation and capital returns still make cash conversion the key creditor test. A current proxy, detailed order-to-revenue conversion, margin delivery and post-quarter cash-flow data would clarify whether the service base and recent wins offset mix and working-capital pressure.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The filings support an issuer-level view of a listed company that has refinanced its post-reorganization debt and continues to return capital, but they do not identify a current controlling shareholder or sponsor. The documented buybacks occur alongside weak nine-month cash conversion, so they reduce liquidity available for working capital and investment; the evidence does not establish that a sponsor directed them or that they breached debt protections. The company’s periodic filings and effective disclosure-control statement support lender visibility, while the absent proxy and current compliance information limit assessment of control rights and covenant capacity. The sponsor and governance risk level is therefore insufficiently established; the actionable focus is the board’s future capital-return policy, post-quarter cash conversion and the use of the remaining authorization.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The company and certain U.S. and Canadian subsidiaries filed prepackaged Chapter 11 cases on June 1, 2023; a Dutch scheme proceeded alongside them. The U.S. court confirmed the plan on July 13, the Dutch court sanctioned its plan on August 2, and both plans became effective on August 11, 2023. The company emerged using fresh-start accounting; the former common shareholders received less than half of the successor’s new common shares. This reset separated the predecessor and successor financial reporting, but the filing does not provide current beneficial-holder percentages.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: On December 18, 2024, Diebold Nixdorf issued USD 950 million of 7.75% senior secured notes due March 2030 and entered a USD 310 million revolving facility due December 18, 2029. The company used the note proceeds, a USD 70 million revolver borrowing and cash on hand to repurchase the emergence term loans, repay the prior revolver and pay related fees and premiums. The new notes and revolver share first-priority collateral; specified subsidiaries guarantee both facilities. The Q3 2026 filing reports that USD 37 million was drawn and repaid on the revolver during the first nine months of 2026, with no revolver balance at quarter-end.

fields.value: Issuer: DIEBOLD NIXDORF, Inc (dbd-28823); as of 2026-11-18. Pathway: credit_snapshot. Scope: synthesize the company’s fundamental credit profile, cash-flow durability, liquidity, refinancing capacity and principal downside through Q3 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Diebold Nixdorf’s service base and funded-debt maturities support creditor resilience, but weak cash conversion and continuing share repurchases are reducing liquidity flexibility. The key near-term test is whether working-capital cash use reverses before taxes and further discretionary capital returns consume the cash buffer.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Revenue grew, but its mix shifted toward Retail: nine-month sales rose 4.3%, with Retail up 21.9% and Banking down 1.9% on the earnings-release presentation. Retail’s lower reported gross margin means growth can add scale while diluting margin if the gap persists.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Cash conversion weakened sharply: nine-month operating cash flow and free cash flow were negative USD 29.3 million and USD 68.5 million, respectively, after positive USD 83.2 million and USD 43.3 million in the prior-year period. Even excluding discrete taxes, the issuer’s free-cash-flow measure remained negative at USD 36.2 million.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Leverage increased mainly because cash fell, not because reported carrying debt surged: carrying-value net debt rose by USD 213.2 million from year-end 2025 to USD 764.4 million, and net leverage reached 2.33x. The company’s own USD 791.5 million net-debt figure uses gross debt before financing fees; the carrying-value measure is used here for leverage.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Adjusted EBITDA is materially above reported EBITDA: the nine-month gap was USD 127.5 million, or 57.95% of reported EBITDA. Restructuring charges, the Turkey operation and an investment impairment account for major adjustments, so reported EBITDA is the more conservative base for leverage and cash-conversion analysis.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - The USD 454.8 million unrestricted cash and net committed availability buffer, alongside known revolver and note maturities in 2029 and 2030, reduces immediate refinancing pressure. It does not establish covenant headroom or the maturity of USD 26.4 million of unidentified other long-term debt.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The negative cash flow is partly affected by inventory and tax timing, rather than a reported EBITDA collapse: cash flow before listed asset-and-liability movements was USD 145.3 million, and management still guides to positive FY2026 free cash flow. Service revenue, customer wins and the absence of a customer above 10% of FY2025 sales also support continuity. Evidence that inventory turns, collections and deferred revenue stabilize and that reported free cash flow recovers without continued large exclusions would improve the view; another period of cash use while repurchases continue would weaken it.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Diebold Nixdorf has an adequate but weakening fundamental profile: global service operations and customer breadth support revenue visibility, while the latest cash conversion and shareholder returns weaken liquidity protection. Nine-month 2026 revenue rose 4.3%, but free cash flow was negative USD 68.5 million; carrying-value net leverage increased to 2.33x as cash declined. Unrestricted cash plus net revolver availability was USD 454.8 million, and the principal notes mature in 2030. This buffer and the absence of a near-term funded maturity mitigate immediate refinancing risk, but the unidentified other-debt maturity, unavailable covenant headroom and further capital returns constrain confidence. A recovery in working capital and positive full-year free cash flow are the main near-term credit tests.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The company sells automation hardware, software and related services to banks and retailers, including ATMs, cash recyclers, point-of-sale systems and self-checkout equipment. Its service and maintenance activities support the installed base, but the filings do not provide renewal rates, contract duration or customer switching data. FY2025 revenue originated mainly in EMEA, with the Americas as the second-largest region; this geographic spread and the lack of any customer above 10% reduce account concentration, while EMEA remains the largest regional exposure.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Services made up 58.7% of nine-month sales, but product sales remained 41.3%; the business is therefore not insulated from equipment demand and delivery cycles. Retail sales increased 21.9% while Banking sales declined 1.9% on the earnings-release GAAP presentation. Reported nine-month Retail gross margin was 21.3% versus Banking at 26.4%; further Retail mix growth can lower the consolidated margin if that differential persists. The Q3 filing shows higher memory costs and an unfavorable regional and product mix pressuring product margin, partly offset by tariff recoveries and pricing actions.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The issuer is a public Delaware corporation with common stock listed on the NYSE. A restructuring replaced the predecessor equity base and introduced fresh-start accounting; current beneficial-owner percentages, sponsor identity, board rights and support commitments are not established in the supplied filings. The issuer also holds minority equity-method interests in two strategic Chinese joint ventures, with disclosed ordinary-course affiliate balances at year-end 2025. For creditors, listed status and regular filings support monitoring, but the absent proxy detail and legal documents prevent an ownership-alignment or structural-subordination conclusion.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Reported revenue growth and the service mix provide some cash-flow visibility, but the absence of contract backlog, renewal and price-pass-through data prevents treating services as fully recurring. Banking demand remains exposed to bank investment cycles and substitution away from cash; Retail growth depends on customer rollouts and store spending. No customer above 10% of annual sales limits single-name concentration, yet it does not establish switching costs or pricing power.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Margin protection is mixed. Nine-month product margin fell as memory costs and mix shifted against the company; customer pricing and tariff recoveries partially offset these pressures. Service margin improved with VAT credits and operating execution; the filings do not establish that VAT credits recur or contractually pass through input costs. The business has investment needs for software and service-fleet modernization, and the filings do not split maintenance from growth spending or fixed from variable costs. This limits the assumed cost cushion under a volume decline.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Nine-month operating cash flow was negative USD 29.3 million, with free cash flow negative USD 68.5 million including discrete taxes; excluding discrete taxes, the issuer’s FCF measure was still negative USD 36.2 million. The cash-flow statement attributes use to inventory, tax and other working-capital movements. Deferred revenue also declined to USD 254.1 million from USD 325.8 million at year-end, reducing customer-funded operating float. Thus EBITDA does not currently translate into reliable debt-service cash without working-capital recovery. No factoring or supplier-finance program is identified in the reviewed filings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Competitive rivalry is credit-relevant because the issuer identifies pricing pressure and new competitors as risks; weaker pricing combined with elevated component costs can compress product margins and reduce cash available for debt service. New entry is less assessable: the company’s product, software and field-service footprint indicates execution requirements, but the filings do not provide market shares or entry economics to measure barriers. Substitution away from cash is a direct threat to ATM usage and Banking hardware demand. Buyer concentration is moderated by the absence of a customer above 10% of sales, but contract terms and renewal rates are unavailable. Supplier power is visible in elevated memory costs; tariff recoveries and pricing actions offset part, not all, of the pressure.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Political and economic factors are material because the issuer identifies tariff changes, geopolitical disruption, currency movements, inflation, and cyclical bank and retailer spending as risks. Tariffs and memory costs can raise product cost, while cash displacement and weak customer capex can reduce Banking demand; both pathways pressure margins and FCF. Cybersecurity and privacy regulation can interrupt service delivery or increase compliance expense, although no event loss is quantified in the filings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The credit-translated SWOT is concise: strengths are the service base, customer breadth and 2029–2030 funded-debt maturities; weaknesses are weak cash conversion, lower-margin Retail mix growth and material adjusted-EBITDA exclusions. Retail wins, service agreements and fleet modernization are possible improvements only if delivered and collected. Threats include cash substitution, component inflation, tariff changes, working-capital outflows and discretionary repurchases competing for liquidity.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Scale and product breadth provide a material operating base, and customer and regional disclosures indicate some diversification; no market-share or peer data supports a sector ranking. Competitive advantage is supported by the installed service base and breadth of equipment and software, but stickiness and price pass-through are not measured. Cost flexibility and margin stability are constrained by product cost inflation, lower-margin Retail growth and unavailable cost-behavior detail. Free-cash-flow stability is weak on the latest nine-month evidence. Liquidity is meaningful at the current date but is being consumed by cash-flow deficits, tax payments and repurchases. Refinancing capacity benefits from the completed refinancing and a 2030 note maturity, while the 2029 revolver, capital-market access and USD 26.4 million unidentified debt remain relevant. Financial policy is creditor-negative when repurchases exceed internally generated cash; current control and covenant capacity are not assessable.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Over the next 12-24 months, management’s reduced FY2026 guidance for revenue, adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow makes recovery dependent on Q4 delivery, collections and tax timing. Across 3-5 years, Retail rollouts, service work and product execution could support demand, but order conversion and margin returns remain unquantified. Credit performance therefore hinges on execution and cash recovery, not a confirmed long-term growth run-rate.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Near-term performance depends on converting the reduced FY2026 outlook into cash; the longer-term opportunity remains conditional on delivering and collecting service and product growth.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: If memory costs remain elevated and bank customers defer equipment spending while Retail growth shifts further toward lower-margin products, Banking revenue and product gross profit would weaken first. Lower volume and unfavorable mix would pressure segment margins; fixed operating costs and service-fleet investment would then limit EBITDA-to-cash conversion. If inventory and tax cash use persist while deferred revenue declines, free cash flow could remain negative and further reduce cash. Continued repurchases would add to that draw, increasing revolver usage and net leverage; a smaller liquidity buffer would make the 2029 revolver refinancing and 2030 notes more sensitive to market access. Management can slow repurchases, manage inventory and collections, defer discretionary investment, and complete the stated non-core exits, but the filings do not quantify available savings, exit proceeds or covenant capacity. Current liquidity and the known maturity profile mitigate immediate pressure; the other-debt maturity remains unidentified, and the evidence is not sufficient to conclude that the company could absorb a prolonged downside without liquidity stress.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The primary downside path is persistent inventory, tax and collection cash use combined with continued buybacks, which would drain the cash buffer, increase revolver reliance and weaken refinancing flexibility before the 2029–2030 maturities.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Overall, Diebold Nixdorf presents an adequate business profile supported by a global service base, customer breadth and a funded maturity profile extending to 2029–2030, but credit quality is constrained by weak cash conversion, working-capital volatility, lower-margin mix and discretionary repurchases. Cash-flow durability is weak on the latest nine-month evidence because operating cash flow and FCF were negative even after excluding discrete taxes from the issuer’s FCF measure. Refinancing capacity will depend on cash recovery, capital-market access and the company’s willingness to retain liquidity. The primary downside path is continued working-capital cash use alongside further capital returns. A more definitive view requires current covenant calculations, the terms and maturity of other debt, current beneficial ownership and evidence on contract renewals and order conversion. No peer data supports a sector-relative ranking.
